newsitem.title: USA: White House says Clinton would veto disaster bill.
newsitem.headline: White House says Clinton would veto disaster bill.

text.p: The White House threatened Tuesday to veto a bill giving relief to disaster victims if Republicans attach a measure to continue federal spending on automatic pilot absent passage of the year's budget.

Office of Management and Budget Director Frank Raines told reporters President Clinton would "veto the bill," if the measure was included. He accused Republicans of acting in bad faith to influence current budget negotiations.
"We believe (it) to be a futile attempt to try to influence the budget negotiations. We believe that this is a bad faith move and we strongly urge them to reverse course," he said.

The so-called permanent continuing resolution sought by Republicans would take the pressure off Congress to approve the annual spending bills as there would no longer be a danger of government shutdown after the Oct. 1 start of a new fiscal year.

These spending bills cover all of the government's activities except mandatory benefit payments and interest on the federal debt. Clinton's veto of spending bills resulted in two federal shutdowns in the winter of 1996 which the public generally blamed on the Republican-led Congress.
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott reacted strongly to the threatened veto. "The president always wants what he wants."

"I am tired of being dragged around ... We can have cooperation and legislative activity or we can go ahead and start the fight. I'm ready to get it on. When it comes to spending and appropriations bills in the budget, as I said, I'll fight on this line all summer," the Mississippi Republican said.

The Republican measure would continue federal spending at 98 percent of this year's level if Congress and the president cannot agree on the 13 regular appropriations bills for the government financial year starting Oct. 1.

The disaster relief bill working its way through Congress would provide $5.5 billion for disaster relief and recovery in 20 states in the upper Midwest, Ohio Valley, Southeast and Pacific Northwest. Most of these states have experienced record-shattering floods.
In addition, it would provide $1.8 billion to rebuild military accounts whose funds have been drawn down by U.S. military operations in Bosnia and southwest Asia.

Raines met with Democrats in the Senate and House to discuss the possibility of reaching a balanced budget agreement but said it would be "remarkable" if they cut a deal in the next 24 hours as Lott said could be possible.
"There's no deal at the moment, and it would be remarkable progress if there was one in 24 hours," Raines told reporters.
Meanwhile, the Senate Appropriations Committee rescheduled to Wednesday its vote on the emergency disaster relief bill when minority Democrats objected to several Republican-crafted provisions.
Appropriations Committee Chairman Ted Stevens said he still hoped to complete Senate action on the bill by May 23 when Congress takes a Memorial Day holiday recess.

The Alaska Republican said Republican leaders wanted the anti-shutdown measure and another controversial provision to stop the administration from using only union labour on construction contracts. Democrats also object to that provision.
A House committee has already approved an $8.4 billion emergency spending bill that will go to the House floor next week for a vote.
